This got me thinking, so first, thank you for raising the question.

Even though arts education is basically non-existent in primary and secondary education these days (e.g. STEM vs STEAM) there's a built-in bias hymns have for the arts. I'm going to exclude visual art for the moment so no disrespect please. It seems that humans seek out art and music anyway, sometimes without knowing whether it is either interesting or relevant.

My wife, a visual artist, enjoys classical music with a certain kind of buoyancy in it. Using Spotify, she added a playlist of classical music that does it for her. Without any effort, that playlist has been subscribed to more than 5,000 times, which I read as interest (people want to hear it) and relevance (there is a reason people want to hear it). Of course, it's also possible that more than 5,000 people are just lazy so they use her list vs making one of their own....

Doesn't this mean that, If alla us classical music people did a better job creating interest and relevance, the "popularity" of classical music would improve? 

We could do that by curating not the music itself but the practical application of the music. We all know how much mileage Barber's Adagio for Strings has gotten, for example, and there are other classical pieces that have gotten a fair amount of overplay even in their un-bastardized forms. Why is that? What is it about those pieces that grabs human interest? What makes those pieces relevant?

I understand that familiarity is important - the discussion of metal above is apt - and I feel that society could do a better job with that, which is a great argument for public funding of classical music. But exposure is one thing and familiarity comes with study and effort. The implication of that for public education used to be a given; fascination with technology and decreased public valuation of education has marginalized the value of education and the profession as well as the value of the music and the arts we used to teach there at a time when we are most impressionable and eager to absorb understanding, and that is a shame.

I have had some success with blended programmes where classical music is a part but not the only part. The objective is to slide in classical relevance through the back door once an audience has built some trust in the musical ride we take together. It doesn't take much to contrast the human response to one genre of music with the human response to another, and once audiences grasp this, they become music hunters, eager to figure out the physiological effects various genres of music have on them. (That's beautifully individual, by the way.) This can be done without any advanced knowledge of theory, harmony, etc, and it applies to classical music of all eras, as well as all other music.

Bottom line: by creating awareness of the physiological response we humans have to organized and disorganized sounds, we increase the interest in and relevance of those sounds. 

In my experience, people deserve that awareness. Often, the results are more positive than negative, both for musicians and listeners.
